t.3.63.1: Bṛhadaśva said: Having abandoned Damayantī, O lord of the people, King Nala saw a great forest fire blazing in the dense wood.
t.3.63.2: There he heard, in the midst of the fire, the voice of some being crying out loudly and again and again, "Run here, Nala! Puṇyaśloka!"
t.3.63.3: Saying "Do not be afraid," Nala entered into the midst of the fire and saw him, the king of serpents, lying there coiled up.
t.3.63.4: Then that serpent, joining his palms in reverence and trembling, said to Nala: "Know me, O king, to be the serpent Karkoṭaka, O lord of men."
t.3.63.5: A brahmarṣi, sinless and of very great austerity, was deceived by me, O lord of men; seized by wrath, he cursed me.
t.3.63.6: Because of his curse I cannot move a single step from this spot. I will tell you what is to your good; you ought to rescue me.
t.3.63.7: I will be your friend; there is no serpent equal to me. I will become light for you; take me up and go quickly.
t.3.63.8: Having spoken thus, that lord of serpents became no bigger than a thumb. Taking him up, Nala went to a place free of the forest fire.
t.3.63.9: Having reached an open place untouched by the fire, the serpent Karkoṭaka spoke again to him as he was about to set him down.
t.3.63.10: Go, O Naiṣadha, counting a few of your own steps; there, great king, I shall bestow on you that good which is the highest.
t.3.63.11: Then, as he began to count, the serpent bit him at the tenth step, and once he was bitten, his form swiftly vanished.
t.3.63.12: Seeing himself transformed, Nala stood there astonished; and the lord of the earth beheld the Nāga, now bearing his own true form.
t.3.63.13: Then the serpent Karkoṭaka, consoling Nala, said: "I have concealed your form, so that people may not recognize you."
t.3.63.14: He on whose account you have been disfigured by great sorrow, O Nala, will dwell within you in misery, tormented by my poison.
t.3.63.15: As long as he, his limbs enveloped by poison, does not release you, so long, great king, will he dwell within you in misery.
t.3.63.16: O lord of men, you are sinless and did not deserve to be wronged by him. Out of anger and indignation toward him, I have made this protection for you.
t.3.63.17: By my grace, O tiger among men, you shall have no fear from fanged beasts, nor from an enemy, nor from those who know brahman, O lord of men.
t.3.63.18: O king, you will suffer no pain caused by poison, and in battles, O lord of kings, you will ever win victory.
t.3.63.19: Go hence, O king, this very day, O lord of the Niṣadhas, to the delightful city of Ayodhyā, into the presence of Ṛtuparṇa, saying, "I am Bāhuka, a charioteer"; for he knows the skill of dice.
t.3.63.20: That glorious king, born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, will give you the secret of the dice in exchange for the secret of horses, and he will also become your friend.
t.3.63.21: When you have become skilled at dice, then you will be joined with good fortune, and you will be reunited with your wife, your kingdom, and your two children; do not set your mind on grief. This I tell you truly.
t.3.63.22: And when you wish to see your own form, O lord of men, then you should call me to mind and put on this garment.
t.3.63.23: "Covered with this garment, you will regain your own form." Having said this, he then gave him a pair of divine garments.
t.3.63.24: Having thus instructed Nala and given him the garment, O Kaurava, the king of the Nāgas then, O king, vanished right there.
